questions.title: AOP Core Concepts
questions.question: What are the core concepts of Spring AOP?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Aspect:** the cross-cutting concern encapsulated as a class
- **Join point:** a point in execution — Spring AOP: only method calls
- **Pointcut:** expression that selects join points where advice applies
- **Advice types:** `@Before`, `@After`, `@Around`, `@AfterReturning`, `@AfterThrowing`
- **Red flag:** not knowing Spring AOP is proxy-based and only intercepts method calls on Spring beans

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring AOP has five core concepts. An **aspect** is a class annotated with `@Aspect` that encapsulates cross-cutting logic — logging, security checks, transaction management. A **join point** is a point in program execution where advice can be applied — in Spring AOP, this is always a method invocation. A **pointcut** is an expression that selects which join points to intercept. **Advice** is the code that runs at a join point, with types: `@Before` (before the method), `@After` (always after), `@Around` (wraps the method), `@AfterReturning` (on success), `@AfterThrowing` (on exception).

Spring AOP is proxy-based — it creates a CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy around your bean. This means it can only intercept method calls made through the Spring proxy. Calling a method within the same class — `this.method()` — bypasses the proxy and AOP doesn't fire.

sections.title: Why Cross-Cutting Concerns Break Clean Architecture — and How AOP Fixes It
sections.content:
Logging, security checks, transaction management, performance monitoring — these concerns cut **across** every layer of your application. Without AOP, you either duplicate the same code in every method, or you build a tangled web of utility calls that obscure the actual business logic. Neither approach scales.

Consider transaction management. Without `@Transactional`, every service method that needs a transaction contains the same boilerplate: get a connection, begin a transaction, try the business logic, commit on success, rollback on failure, close the connection. The transaction logic is identical across hundreds of methods — but you can't extract it cleanly because it wraps the business logic, not precedes or follows it.

AOP solves this by separating **what** a cross-cutting concern does (the advice) from **where** it applies (the pointcut). You define the behavior once — "wrap the method in a transaction" — and declare where it applies — "every public method in a `@Service` class." Spring weaves them together at runtime through proxies, so your service methods contain only business logic while transactions happen invisibly around them.

The terminology maps to this mental model: an **aspect** is a cross-cutting concern packaged as a class. A **join point** is a place where the aspect can apply (in Spring AOP, always a method execution). A **pointcut** is a predicate that selects specific join points. **Advice** is the actual code that runs — before, after, or around the join point. Spring creates a **proxy** around the target bean, and the proxy intercepts method calls to execute the advice.

questions.title: @Around Advice
questions.question: How does @Around advice work and when should you use it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Most powerful advice type:** can control whether method executes, modify args, modify return value
- **`ProceedingJoinPoint`:** the object that lets you actually call the target method
- **Must call `proceed()`:** or the target method never runs — common mistake
- **Can modify the return value:** aspect can change what the caller sees
- **Red flag:** using `@Around` when `@Before` or `@After` would suffice — overkill

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Around` advice is the most powerful type — it wraps the entire method execution and can control whether the method runs at all, modify the arguments passed in, and modify or replace the return value. It receives a `ProceedingJoinPoint` parameter and must call `proceed()` to execute the actual target method.

This makes `@Around` suitable for things like timing method execution — you capture time before `proceed()` and after, and log the duration. Or implementing a retry mechanism — call `proceed()` in a loop with backoff on exception. Or implementing a circuit breaker — check a flag before calling `proceed()`.

Be careful not to forget `proceed()` — if your `@Around` advice throws an exception before calling it, the target method silently never runs. Always ensure `proceed()` is called in the correct branch of your logic.

sections.title: The Most Powerful AOP Advice — and the Most Dangerous If Misused
sections.content:
`@Around` is the only advice type that controls whether the target method executes at all. It receives a `ProceedingJoinPoint`, calls `proceed()` to invoke the original method, and can act on both the input and the output. This makes it the foundation of Spring's most important features: `@Transactional` wraps the method in a transaction, `@Cacheable` checks the cache before calling the method and skips it on cache hits, and `@Async` delegates execution to another thread.

The power comes with a critical responsibility: **you must call `proceed()`** in the normal flow. Forget it, and the target method silently never executes. No error, no warning — the proxy simply returns whatever your advice returns (often `null`). This is the most common `@Around` bug, and it's especially insidious because it manifests as missing side effects rather than errors.

`@Around` is the right choice when your advice needs to wrap the method call — control execution, transform the return value, handle exceptions, or measure elapsed time. For simpler scenarios — logging before a method runs, or auditing the return value — `@Before` and `@AfterReturning` are clearer because they communicate intent without the risk of forgetting `proceed()`.

The decision rule: if you need access to both the input and the output, or need to prevent execution, use `@Around`. If you only need one side, use the simpler advice type.

questions.title: Pointcut Expressions
questions.question: How do you write pointcut expressions in Spring AOP?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`execution()`:** most common — match method signatures
- **`@annotation()`:** match methods annotated with a specific annotation
- **`within()`:** match all methods within a type or package
- **Combining expressions:** `&&`, `||`, `!` operators
- **Red flag:** only knowing `execution()` — `@annotation()` is critical for custom AOP

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Pointcut expressions use AspectJ syntax to select join points. The most common designator is `execution()`, which matches method signatures. The format is `execution(modifiers return-type declaring-type.method-name(params) throws-clause)`, where `*` is a wildcard and `..` matches any params.

`@annotation()` is extremely useful — it matches any method annotated with the specified annotation. This is the basis for custom annotations like `@Retryable` or `@Audited` — you create the annotation, write a pointcut matching it, and any method annotated gets the cross-cutting behaviour.

`within()` matches all methods within a package or type — useful when you want to apply logic to an entire layer without specifying each class. You combine designators with `&&`, `||`, and `!` to build precise selectors.

sections.title: The Pattern Language That Decides Where Your Aspect Fires
sections.content:
A pointcut expression is a predicate that selects which method executions an aspect applies to. Get it wrong, and your aspect either fires on every method in the application (destroying performance), misses the methods it should target (appearing broken), or — worst case — matches methods in third-party libraries and causes baffling side effects.

Spring AOP supports several pointcut designators, but three dominate production use: **`execution()`** matches by method signature pattern, **`@annotation()`** matches by the presence of an annotation, and **`within()`** matches by declaring class. The rest — `args()`, `target()`, `this()`, `@within()`, `@args()` — are niche tools for advanced scenarios.

The most important thing to understand is that Spring AOP pointcuts only match **Spring-managed bean methods**. A pointcut expression that would match a method on a non-bean object does nothing — Spring AOP works through proxies, and non-beans don't get proxied. Additionally, Spring AOP only intercepts **public methods** by default when using JDK dynamic proxies. CGLIB proxies can intercept protected and package-private methods, but private methods are always excluded.

A well-designed pointcut is **narrow and intentional**. `execution(* *.*(..))` matches everything — every method on every bean. This causes performance issues and unexpected behavior. Prefer annotation-based pointcuts (`@annotation(Timed)`) for explicitly opt-in behavior, or tightly scoped `execution()` patterns for convention-based behavior.

questions.title: @Transactional and AOP
questions.question: How does @Transactional work under the hood using AOP?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`TransactionInterceptor` is the aspect:** wraps `@Transactional` methods
- **Proxy-based:** `@Transactional` only works on Spring beans called through the proxy
- **Self-invocation problem:** `this.method()` bypasses the proxy — transaction not started
- **Checked vs unchecked exceptions:** only unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) trigger rollback by default
- **Red flag:** not knowing self-invocation breaks `@Transactional` — most common Spring production bug

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Transactional` is implemented entirely via AOP. When you annotate a method, Spring's `AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource` detects it during context startup and `TransactionInterceptor` is registered as an around advice for that method.

At runtime, when you call a `@Transactional` method on a Spring bean, you're actually calling a method on the CGLIB proxy. The proxy calls `TransactionInterceptor`, which starts a transaction before calling your actual method, then commits on success or rolls back on exception.

The self-invocation problem is the most common `@Transactional` bug: if `methodA()` calls `this.methodB()` within the same class, `methodB()`'s `@Transactional` annotation is ignored because you're not going through the proxy. The fix is to put `methodB()` in a separate Spring bean.

sections.title: The Proxy-Based Transaction That Silently Fails on Self-Invocation
sections.content:
`@Transactional` is Spring's most used AOP feature — and its most misunderstood. Developers annotate a method, trust that it runs in a transaction, and move on. Then a bug appears: data was partially committed when it should have been rolled back, or a method annotated `@Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW)` didn't actually get a new transaction. The root cause is almost always the same: the developer didn't understand that `@Transactional` works through a **proxy**, not through bytecode modification.

When Spring finds a bean with `@Transactional` methods, it creates a proxy that wraps the bean. When you call a `@Transactional` method through the proxy, the proxy opens a transaction, delegates to the real method, and commits or rolls back based on the outcome. The key phrase is "through the proxy" — if the call doesn't go through the proxy, no transaction management happens.

This is why **self-invocation** is the number one `@Transactional` bug. When a method inside the same class calls another method using `this.annotatedMethod()`, the call bypasses the proxy entirely. The `@Transactional` annotation is invisible. The method runs without a transaction (or inherits the caller's transaction, if one exists), regardless of its annotation.

The second most common issue is **exception type**. By default, `@Transactional` only rolls back on unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException` and its subclasses). Checked exceptions cause a **commit**, not a rollback. If your method throws `IOException` and you expect a rollback, you need `@Transactional(rollbackFor = IOException.class)` — otherwise Spring commits the partial changes.

sections.title: What the Proxy Does: The Transaction Lifecycle Around Your Method
sections.content:
When a call arrives at the `@Transactional` proxy, the following sequence occurs:

1. **Check propagation** — Does a transaction already exist? Based on the propagation level (`REQUIRED`, `REQUIRES_NEW`, `SUPPORTS`, etc.), the proxy either joins the existing transaction, creates a new one, or proceeds without one.

2. **Obtain a connection** — The proxy gets a database connection from the `DataSource` and binds it to the current thread via `TransactionSynchronizationManager`. All data access on this thread uses this connection, ensuring all operations are in the same transaction.

3. **Disable auto-commit** — The connection's auto-commit is turned off so that multiple SQL statements are grouped into one transaction.

4. **Invoke the target method** — The proxy calls your actual method. Your method's `@Autowired` repository calls use the thread-bound connection.

5. **Commit or rollback** — If the method returns normally, the proxy commits. If it throws an unchecked exception (by default), the proxy rolls back. If it throws a checked exception, the proxy **commits** — unless you explicitly configure `rollbackFor`.

6. **Release the connection** — The connection is unbound from the thread and returned to the pool.

The thread-binding in step 2 is crucial. It's why `@Transactional` doesn't work with `@Async` out of the box — the async method runs on a different thread, which doesn't have the transaction-bound connection. It's also why `@Transactional` and reactive (`WebFlux`) don't mix — reactive execution switches threads freely, breaking the thread-bound connection model.

questions.title: Custom Annotation with AOP
questions.question: How do you create a custom annotation backed by AOP?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Create annotation → Create aspect → Pointcut on annotation:** the three-step pattern
- **`@annotation()` pointcut:** matches methods annotated with your custom annotation
- **Access annotation attributes via `JoinPoint` reflection or `@annotation` binding:** to read annotation values
- **Common examples:** `@RateLimit`, `@Audited`, `@Cacheable` equivalent, `@Retry`
- **Red flag:** creating the annotation without the `@Retention(RUNTIME)` — annotation invisible at runtime

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Creating a custom AOP-backed annotation involves three steps. First, define the annotation with `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` — without RUNTIME retention, the annotation is stripped at compile time and the aspect can't see it. Second, create an `@Aspect` class with a pointcut that matches `@annotation(yourAnnotation)`. Third, write advice that uses the annotation's attributes.

To access the annotation's attributes in the advice, you use `@annotation` parameter binding — declare the annotation type as a method parameter with the same name as the `@annotation()` binding, and Spring passes the actual annotation instance. Then you read its attributes normally.

This pattern is how Spring implements `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, and `@Async` — and it's how you can add your own framework-quality annotations to your application.

sections.title: Building Your Own @Transactional: Custom Annotations Backed by Aspects
sections.content:
The pattern behind `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, and `@Retryable` is the same: a custom annotation marks a method, and an aspect detects the annotation and wraps the method with behavior. You can build your own cross-cutting annotations following exactly this pattern — and it's one of the most valuable Spring skills for eliminating boilerplate in production codebases.

The typical candidates for custom AOP annotations are: **rate limiting** (reject calls that exceed a threshold), **retry logic** (automatically retry on transient failures), **distributed locking** (acquire a lock before execution), **audit logging** (record who called what, when), and **circuit breaking** (fail fast when a dependency is down).

Without AOP, each of these concerns gets implemented inline: every method that needs retry logic has a `for` loop with a `try/catch` and a `Thread.sleep()`. When the retry strategy changes — exponential backoff instead of fixed delay — you update dozens of methods. With a custom `@Retryable` annotation and an aspect, you update one class.

The pattern is three pieces: the **annotation** (the marker), the **aspect** (the behavior), and optionally an **`@Enable*` annotation** or auto-configuration that activates the aspect. The annotation should carry configuration as attributes — retry count, delay, exception types — so each use site can customize the behavior without modifying the aspect.

questions.title: CGLIB vs JDK Dynamic Proxy
questions.question: What is the difference between CGLIB and JDK dynamic proxies in Spring AOP?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **JDK proxy:** works only if the target implements an interface
- **CGLIB proxy:** subclasses the target class — works even without an interface
- **Spring Boot default: CGLIB** since Spring 4 (Boot 2+) — you rarely need to worry about this
- **`final` class or method breaks CGLIB:** can't subclass a final class
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@Transactional` on a final method silently doesn't work

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring AOP can create proxies two ways. JDK dynamic proxies use Java's `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` — they only work if the target bean implements at least one interface, and the proxy implements those same interfaces. CGLIB (Code Generation Library) proxies work by subclassing the target class at runtime, so they work even if the class implements no interface.

Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies since Spring 4.3. This means your `@Service` classes don't need to implement interfaces for AOP to work — which is a good thing because most classes don't.

The CGLIB constraint is that it can't subclass `final` classes or override `final` methods. If you annotate a `final` method with `@Transactional` or `@Cacheable`, the annotation is silently ignored — CGLIB can't intercept it. This is a subtle bug because there's no error at startup.

sections.title: The Two Proxy Strategies Spring Chooses Between — and Why You Usually Don't Care
sections.content:
Spring AOP intercepts method calls through proxies, and it has two mechanisms for creating them: **JDK dynamic proxies** and **CGLIB proxies**. JDK proxies implement the same interfaces as the target bean — they work through interface-based polymorphism. CGLIB proxies create a subclass of the target bean — they work through inheritance.

The distinction mattered more in older Spring versions, where the proxy choice affected which methods could be intercepted and whether you could cast to the concrete class. Since Spring Boot 2.0, **CGLIB is the default**, and for most applications the proxy mechanism is invisible — you never think about it, and it just works.

The reason Spring Boot switched to CGLIB as the default is practical: JDK proxies require the bean to implement at least one interface. If your `@Service` class doesn't implement an interface (which is common in modern Spring applications), JDK proxies can't be used. CGLIB has no such requirement — it subclasses the concrete class directly.

Understanding the difference still matters for edge cases: final classes and methods can't be proxied by CGLIB (because it uses subclassing, and you can't subclass `final`). JDK proxies can't intercept calls to methods not declared on the interface. And both mechanisms share the same self-invocation limitation — `this.method()` bypasses the proxy regardless of which type is used.

sections.title: JDK Dynamic Proxy vs. CGLIB: When the Difference Matters
sections.content:
For most Spring Boot applications, the proxy type is invisible. This table captures the cases where it matters — primarily edge cases around class design and method visibility.

| Concern | JDK Dynamic Proxy | CGLIB Proxy |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Implements target's interfaces | Subclasses the target class |
| Requirement | Bean must implement an interface | No interface needed |
| Final classes | Works (proxies the interface) | Cannot proxy — Spring throws error |
| Final methods | Intercepted (via interface) | Not intercepted — bypasses proxy |
| Protected methods | Not intercepted | Intercepted |
| Self-invocation | Bypasses proxy | Bypasses proxy |
| Type casting | Cast to interface only (not concrete class) | Cast to concrete class works |
| Default in Spring Boot 2+ | No | Yes |

The **final method** row is the most surprising. If you mark a method as `final` on a class proxied by CGLIB, the method is **not intercepted** — the subclass can't override it. If that method has `@Transactional`, the transaction silently doesn't happen. There's no error or warning. Kotlin classes are `final` by default, which is why the `kotlin-spring` compiler plugin automatically opens Spring-managed classes and their methods.

questions.title: @Async and AOP
questions.question: How does @Async work and what are its limitations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Async` executes the method in a different thread:** returns immediately to caller
- **`@EnableAsync` required:** on a `@Configuration` class to enable it
- **Return type:** must be `void`, `Future<T>`, or `CompletableFuture<T>` — not a direct value
- **Self-invocation doesn't work:** same proxy limitation as `@Transactional`
- **Red flag:** not knowing about the default thread pool — unbounded `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` by default, always configure a bounded executor

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Async` is another AOP-based feature. When you call an `@Async` method on a Spring bean, the proxy intercepts the call and submits the method execution to a thread pool, returning immediately. The actual method runs asynchronously on a different thread.

To use it, you need `@EnableAsync` on a configuration class, and methods must return `void`, `Future<T>`, or `CompletableFuture<T>` — you can't return a plain value because the method hasn't finished yet.

The critical production concern is the default executor. Without configuration, Spring uses `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor`, which creates a new thread for every invocation — effectively unbounded. Under any real load, this will exhaust system resources. Always configure a bounded `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` with sensible limits.

sections.title: The Thread Boundary That Breaks @Transactional, SecurityContext, and MDC
sections.content:
`@Async` moves method execution to a different thread, and that thread boundary breaks every thread-bound context in Spring. `@Transactional` binds transactions to the calling thread — an async method runs on a new thread without the transaction. `SecurityContextHolder` stores the authenticated user in a `ThreadLocal` — the async thread doesn't have it. `MDC` (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for logging correlation IDs — also thread-local, also missing in the async thread.

This isn't a bug; it's a consequence of how `@Async` works. The AOP proxy intercepts the method call, submits it to a thread pool as a `Runnable`, and returns immediately. The caller gets a `Future` (or `CompletableFuture`) representing the eventual result. The method body runs later, on a pool thread, completely detached from the caller's thread context.

`@Async` requires `@EnableAsync` on a configuration class — without it, the annotation is silently ignored. The method must be called through the proxy — **self-invocation bypasses `@Async`** just like it bypasses `@Transactional`. And the method should return `void`, `Future<T>`, or `CompletableFuture<T>` — returning any other type silently discards the return value because the caller doesn't wait for the result.

The most dangerous misconfiguration is using `@Async` without a custom thread pool. Spring's default is `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor`, which creates a **new thread for every call** with no upper bound. Under load, this creates thousands of threads, exhausting memory and causing the JVM to crash. Always configure a bounded `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`.

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **AOP-based:** proxy intercepts, checks cache before calling method
- **`@EnableCaching` required:** enables caching abstraction
- **SpEL for cache key:** `#id`, `#user.id`, `#root.method.name`
- **`@CacheEvict` and `@CachePut`:** cache invalidation and update
- **Red flag:** not knowing self-invocation bypasses the cache — same proxy limitation

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Cacheable` is another AOP-based feature. When a `@Cacheable` method is called through a Spring proxy, the `CacheInterceptor` checks if the result is already in the cache for the computed key. If it is, it returns the cached value without calling the actual method. If not, it calls the method, caches the result, and returns it.

The cache key is computed from the method parameters by default, or via a SpEL expression. `#id` resolves to the method parameter named `id`. `#user.email` navigates into a parameter's field. You can also use `#root.method.name` or `#root.target` for method-level metadata.

`@CacheEvict` removes entries from the cache — use it on write operations. `@CachePut` always executes the method and updates the cache — use it to keep cache fresh after an update.

sections.title: The Invisible Cache Hit That Skips Your Method Entirely
sections.content:
`@Cacheable` is an `@Around` advice that checks a cache before calling your method. On a cache hit, **your method never executes** — the proxy returns the cached value directly. On a cache miss, the method runs, and the result is stored in the cache for future calls. This behavior is invisible at the call site, which is both the power and the danger.

The danger is that developers forget the method is skipped on cache hits. A method that logs "processing request," updates a counter, or records an audit event does none of those things on a cache hit — because the method body never runs. Side effects in `@Cacheable` methods are unreliable by design.

Spring's cache abstraction is provider-agnostic: `@Cacheable` works with `ConcurrentHashMap` (in-memory, single-JVM), Caffeine (in-memory with eviction), Redis (distributed), EhCache, and any JSR-107 provider. You choose the provider via configuration; the annotations stay the same.

The most common production mistake is using `@Cacheable` without understanding key generation. By default, Spring uses all method parameters as the cache key. Two calls with the same parameters return the same cached result — even if they should differ based on the authenticated user, the tenant, or some other context not passed as a parameter. If your method's result depends on something other than its parameters, you need a custom `key` expression.

questions.title: Aspect Ordering
questions.question: How do you control the order in which aspects execute?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Order(n)`:** lower number = outer advice (runs first for before, last for after)
- **`Ordered` interface:** alternative to `@Order`
- **Spring's built-in order:** `@Transactional` runs at `Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE` by default
- **Advice execution model:** aspects nest like concentric rings — entry order determines exit order too
- **Red flag:** thinking higher `@Order` number means higher priority — it's the opposite (lower = higher priority)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When multiple aspects apply to the same join point, their execution order matters — especially for around advice, where the order determines nesting. `@Order(n)` on an aspect class controls this, with lower numbers executing first (outermost in the call stack).

Think of aspects as concentric rings. The aspect with `@Order(1)` is the outermost ring — its `@Before` code runs first, and its `@After` code runs last. `@Order(2)` is the next ring, and so on. The target method is at the center.

Spring's built-in aspects have defined orders. `@Transactional` defaults to `Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE` (runs innermost). Security aspects run at high priority (outermost). If you add a logging aspect, you typically want it to run outside the transaction — lower order number than the transactional aspect.

sections.title: When Multiple Aspects Wrap the Same Method — and Order Decides Whether It Works
sections.content:
When a method has both `@Transactional` and `@Cacheable`, or a custom `@Retry` annotation alongside `@Transactional`, the execution order of these aspects determines whether the combination works correctly or fails silently. If retry wraps the transaction, each retry attempt gets a fresh transaction — correct behavior for retrying transient database failures. If the transaction wraps retry, all retry attempts share one transaction — and a failure that triggers retry might have already corrupted the transaction's state.

Spring uses the `@Order` annotation (or the `Ordered` interface) on aspect classes to determine execution priority. **Lower numbers execute first** (outermost in the proxy chain). An aspect with `@Order(1)` wraps an aspect with `@Order(2)`, which wraps the target method. Think of it as concentric rings: the lowest-order aspect is the outermost ring.

Without explicit ordering, the execution order of aspects is **undefined** — Spring makes no guarantees. This means the same application might behave differently across restarts if aspect registration order happens to change. For any combination of aspects where order matters, explicit `@Order` values are required.

The advice types within a single aspect also have a defined order. For `@Around` advice, the code before `proceed()` runs in declaration order, and the code after `proceed()` runs in reverse order — like nested try-finally blocks. Across aspects, the outermost aspect's "before" code runs first and its "after" code runs last.

questions.title: Spring AOP vs AspectJ
questions.question: What is the difference between Spring AOP and AspectJ?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Spring AOP: proxy-based, runtime, method calls on Spring beans only**
- **AspectJ: compile-time or load-time weaving, any join point (field access, constructors, static methods)**
- **Spring uses AspectJ annotations:** `@Aspect`, `@Before`, `@Around` — but with Spring's proxy engine
- **When AspectJ is needed:** intercepting non-Spring objects, constructors, field access, static methods
- **Red flag:** thinking Spring AOP IS AspectJ — Spring uses AspectJ annotations with its own proxy engine

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring AOP and full AspectJ are often confused because Spring uses AspectJ's annotation syntax — `@Aspect`, `@Before`, `@Around` — but uses its own proxy-based engine, not AspectJ's weaver.

Spring AOP intercepts method calls on Spring-managed beans through CGLIB or JDK proxies. It can only intercept public method calls made through the proxy — not field access, not constructor calls, not methods called via `this`, and not non-Spring objects.

Full AspectJ does compile-time or load-time weaving — it actually modifies bytecode. This means it can intercept anything: field reads/writes, constructor calls, static methods, private methods. It can also advise non-Spring objects — domain objects created with `new`.

For 95% of use cases in a Spring application, Spring AOP is sufficient. You'd use full AspectJ when you need to advise non-Spring beans, intercept constructors, or intercept field access.

sections.title: Why Spring AOP Is 'Good Enough' for 99% of Applications
sections.content:
Spring AOP and AspectJ are both AOP implementations that use the same annotation syntax (`@Aspect`, `@Before`, `@Around`), but they work through fundamentally different mechanisms. Spring AOP uses **runtime proxies** — wrapper objects that intercept method calls. AspectJ uses **compile-time or load-time weaving** — it modifies bytecode to insert advice directly into the target class.

This difference has cascading implications. Spring AOP can only intercept public method executions on Spring-managed beans. It can't intercept constructor calls, field access, or private method calls. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy. These limitations exist because proxies can only intercept calls that go through them — internal calls and non-method join points are invisible.

AspectJ has none of these limitations. It weaves advice directly into bytecode, so it can intercept constructors, field reads/writes, static methods, private methods, and self-invocation. It can even aspect classes that aren't managed by Spring.

Despite these advantages, **Spring AOP is the right choice for the vast majority of applications**. Its limitations rarely matter in practice — most cross-cutting concerns (transactions, caching, logging, security) apply to public service methods, which Spring AOP handles perfectly. AspectJ adds significant build complexity (a special compiler or load-time weaving agent), harder debugging (woven bytecode is opaque), and a learning curve that doesn't pay off unless you genuinely need its extra capabilities.

sections.title: Spring AOP vs. AspectJ: Capabilities, Costs, and When to Switch
sections.content:
The comparison comes down to a trade-off: Spring AOP is simpler but limited to proxy-based method interception. AspectJ is more powerful but adds build complexity and makes debugging harder.

| Concern | Spring AOP | AspectJ |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Runtime proxies (JDK / CGLIB) | Compile-time or load-time bytecode weaving |
| Join points | Public method execution only | Methods, constructors, fields, static methods |
| Self-invocation | Bypasses proxy — advice doesn't fire | Works — bytecode is woven into the class |
| Spring bean required | Yes — only proxied beans | No — any class, even non-Spring |
| Build setup | None — works out of the box | Requires AspectJ compiler or weaving agent |
| Performance overhead | Per-call proxy delegation | Near-zero — woven into bytecode |
| Debugging | Proxy chain visible in stack trace | Woven code harder to trace |
| Typical use | Transactions, caching, logging, security | Domain model aspects, fine-grained interception |

Switch to AspectJ only when you hit a concrete limitation of Spring AOP: you need to intercept self-invocation without refactoring, you need to aspect non-Spring-managed classes, or you need constructor or field-level interception. For everything else, Spring AOP's simplicity and zero-config setup make it the pragmatic choice.
